description: Software engineer in Toronto (Python, FastAPI, React, Claude API) building an AI dashboard for Flame in Freefall. It pulls NASA's microgravity combustion data into one place, with AI summaries and rankings for Moon and Mars fire safety. I'm covering the data pipeline and AI. Looking for a designer, someone to shape the demo and pitch, and anyone with a physics or aerospace background to sanity-check results.
summary: EMBER brings 37 NASA documents, 133 microgravity test records and 8 research summaries into one place a fire-safety researcher can question. Ask in plain English, for example what happened to SIBAL, a cotton and fiberglass fabric, at 18.7% oxygen and 2 cm/s. EMBER returns the closest real NASA tests, what happened in them, and the exact page and quote behind each claim. A simulator then shows those conditions and rates them green, yellow or red for how closely real tests cover them. Moon, Mars and untested conditions show red, because every test in the data was run in microgravity. When the evidence runs out, EMBER says “not found” instead of guessing. It supports material choice and test planning for the Flame in Freefall challenge. It is not a safety certification.
details:
What it does. EMBER is an evidence tool for spacecraft fire safety, built for the NASA Space Apps “Flame in Freefall” challenge. Researchers ask questions about how fabrics and other materials burn in spacecraft conditions. Answers come first from our own structured test table and the document text, so they are fast and traceable. Every claim links to the NASA document, the page, and the supporting quote. If a question is missing airflow, has no unit, or misspells the material, EMBER asks a follow-up before answering.

The simulator and the rating. Oxygen, airflow, pressure, gravity and material sliders sit under an animated flame. The rating compares your conditions with real tests. Green means a test within 0.5 oxygen points and 2 cm/s. Yellow means within 2 points and 10 cm/s. Red means outside that, or any gravity other than microgravity. The flame animation is illustrative. It follows the outcome class recorded for the nearest test, and the strip is schematic, not a measure of time or distance.

Data. We used NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics records (BASS, BASS-II, Saffire), NASA technical reports, and conference papers on NASA experiments. That’s 133 test rows: 129 from BASS-II and 4 from Saffire VI. Of those, 34 have outcomes we reviewed against the source. None report a flame spread rate, and the tool says so when asked.

Tools. React, Three.js and Tailwind for the interface. FastAPI and BM25 search for the backend. PyMuPDF to read the PDFs. Gemini and Claude are used only as a fallback when local data cannot answer, or when the user ticks “Search NASA live”.

What is creative. Most tools would summarize these reports. Ours maps where the evidence is thin and refuses to answer past it. A researcher can see not only what NASA found, but what NASA has not tested.

Limits. Most of the test rows are PMMA plastic, not fabric. The fabric rows are SIBAL (28) and Nomex (4). Gravity other than microgravity has no data, and the tool does not estimate it. The flame is not a physics simulation.
